To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The relationship between brainECFs and CSF concentrations of P-glycoprotein substrates is significantly influenced by P-gp functionality and therefore requires knowledge on P-gp functionality to be predicted”.

‘the relationship between CSF and unbound brainECFlow concentrations of a drug is significantly influenced by the functionality of P-glycoprotein, and therefore the prediction of human unbound brain target site concentrations on the basis of CSF concentrations of P-glycopyrotein substrates is not valid’.

the brain extracellular-to-cerebrospinal-fluid concentration ratio is a function of the blood-to-cerebro-spinal-fluid ratio and the blood-to-brain extracellular-fluid ratio, which in turn are a function of the activity of P-glycoprotein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the complex relationship between brain target site, CSF and unbound plasma concentrations, and its implications for the prediction of CNS target site exposure in man.
the development of a systems-based pharmacodynamic model that is useful to predict human brain target site exposure on the basis of plasma and CSF data.
the question whether human CSF can be considered as a surrogate for brainECF concentrations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CSF is a poor surrogate for brain target site concentrations in humans.
CSF is not a good enough surrogate for brainECF, and that brainECF concentrations are the best surrogate for brain target site concentrations.
CSF concentrations may be a valid surrogate for brainECF concentrations, provided that P-gp is not functional.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brainECF is a better surrogate for the brain target site than CSF, and that the brainECF-to-CSF ratio is not a constant, but a variable depending on P-gp functionality.
CSF concentrations of P-gP substrates are not a good surrogate for human brainECF concentrations, unless P-gp functionality has been determined.
CSF concentrations can be a good surrogate for brainECF concentrations, if the drug is not a P-gp substrate, and/or if P-gp is fully functional.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CSF is a very unreliable surrogate for brainECF.
the use of CSF concentrations as a surrogate for brain target site concentrations in humans should be done with caution.
CSF concentrations are a poor predictor of brainECF exposure, and that the prediction of human target site CNS concentrations is a challenge.
